Sports.title: Thomas Frank earns first Crystal Palace win as McNeil cuts down Real Sociedad
Sports.summary: Football seasons can pivot on certain moments and Thomas Frank will hope that Crystal Palace’s turning point came 17 minutes from full time here. Deservedly trailing to Mamadou Sarr’s goal having been second best throughout against Real Sociedad, this game – and perhaps the south London club’s entire trajectory – was turned on its head after Jon Martín was sent off for denying Jean-Philippe Mateta an equaliser. The France striker made no mistake with his penalty before Dwight McNeil – who made up for scoring an own goal in Saturday’s defeat by Coventry capped an extraordinary comeback in Frank’s first home match since succeeding Pierre Sage. Despite Yéremy Pino’s saved penalty in stoppage time and a number of other chances that were squandered, Dean Henderson pulled off a stunning late save to seal the victory and revive Palace’s Europa League campaign. Suddenly Palace have hope where there appeared to be none and the Premier League’s bottom side will head into Sunday’s crucial showdown with Hull with a spring in their step. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Mammy Goose is well and truly cooked in Glasgow’s incredibly random Aladdin
Culture.summary: King’s theatre, Glasgow The offensive stereotypes have been ditched but this glitzy panto starring Elaine C Smith shoehorns in plenty of irrelevant material Staging a traditional Aladdin in 2026 is problematic. All those laundry scenes, acrobatics and faux Chinese names have the unpleasant whiff of orientalism. In that sense, it is good to see this glitzy mainstream panto, scripted by Alan McHugh for Crossroads, ditching all that. If only it had not thrown the genie out with the bath water. Stereotypes aside, Aladdin can still be a gripping coming-of-age story about greed and gullibility, poverty and power. The stakes can be loaded with deceit, jeopardy and cunning. In this version, set in the land of Pantomania, almost none of that survives. Continue reading...

Culture.title: You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?
Culture.summary: The Iranian film-maker’s 1990 tale of impersonation and deception happens to be a favourite movie of the Elizabeth Holmes docufiction’s co-director Lance Oppenheim • NB: This article contains spoilers You’re probably sick of hearing how You Can See Everything , about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is the buzziest, coolest, 100% freshest film of the year, but coming out of the screening last week, I couldn’t help but wonder whether Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had been watching a lot of 90s Iranian cinema. And one film in particular: Close-Up, by Abbas Kiarostami. If it feels as if You Can See Everything blends truth, lies, fiction and documentary in mind-bending new ways until you’re no longer sure what the hell you’re watching, then Kiarostami, who died in 2016, practically invented this mode 36 years ago. The context could not be more different – analogue 90s Tehran rather than tech-drunk 2020s California – but the themes are the same: Close-Up is a strange story of impersonation, deception and performance, made even stranger by the film-maker’s deliberate meddling. Continue reading...

The film star, 77, had appealed last year against an investigating magistrate’s ruling that he should stand criminal trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting Charlotte Arnould on two occasions, but judges said on Thursday proceedings should go ahead. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations.
